title: Mabli and the Missing Spark
markdown:
The snow bit at Mabli’s ears, sharp and tasting of distant pine.

“Right then, Ripple,” she hummed, a low thrum against the wind. “Flicker’s vanished. And knowing Flicker, he’s picked the absolute worst spot to hide.”

Ripple, her newt of glistening slime and silent wit, flicked his tail from her shoulder. Flicker, her prized spark-lizard, had pulled this disappearing act before: behind a grumpy grimoire, inside a forgotten kettle. This felt different. The Whispering Peaks loomed, a jagged scar of snow-capped summits, secrets for the wind.

Mabli adjusted her spectacles. Her mind was not built for fanfare, but for neat satisfying thunks as thoughts clicked into place.

“Obstacle one.” A steep snow drift. “Needs a strategic shuffle.” She produced a smooth worn stone and nudged the snow. It slid away, revealing a tiny ramp. Simple. Effective.

Most witches in these highlands kept cats, or grumpy owls. Mabli had Flicker, whose sparks lit the dark, and Ripple, better company than most humans. Ripple’s dappled green, usually slick with dew, now glistened with frost. His gaze stayed sharp.

Villages clung to cliffs like hardy moss. Cragfoot hummed with forgotten magic and peculiar crafts. Home of Agnes Pendle, the Puzzle-Witch, master of riddles and elaborate metaphor. Mabli, pragmatist, needed a riddle-solver to find an adventurous spark-lizard.

“Agnes Pendle?” she asked at a stall piled with glittering ice crystals. The rosy-cheeked apple seller cackled.

“The Puzzle-Witch. Be warned. She makes every problem sound like a legendary quest.”

Agnes Pendle’s cottage was a whirlwind. Gears clanked, orbs spun, scarves billowed like a captured gale. Agnes herself was a blur.

“A lost spark-lizard, you say? Ah, this is no mere disappearance. This is a descent into the Obsidian Labyrinth of Unfound Things. A quest of epic proportions.”

Mabli’s spectacles slid. “He’s probably just under a loose floorboard, Agnes. Could you lend me a very bright light? Flicker gets flustered in the dark, and his sparks aren’t as reliable when he’s worried.”

Agnes waved a dismissive hand, nearly sending tiny bells tumbling. “A light? Nonsense. We must summon the Whispering Winds. Or brew a potion of Temporal Rediscovery under the forgotten moon.”

Ripple let out a small disapproving croak. A tiny amphibian sigh.

Mabli, puzzle-box mind cataloguing, noticed a small cluttered corner, stark against the chaotic brilliance. Spools of thread: fiery reds, sunshine yellows, deep ocean blues. A weaving loom. Carved wooden pieces. Peeking from behind a practical magnifying glass: a single bright spark. Flicker’s spark.

Flicker was not lost. He was crafting. Agnes’s hidden corner was inspiring. He loved bright colours, especially her fetching scarlet and gold threads. A detour to procure materials for an ambitious nest. The inconvenient hiding place was a strategic procurement mission for artisanal nest materials.

Agnes, lost in legendary quests, had not noticed prize thread disappearing, or the subtle scratching from her curio cabinet. Mabli steered her away from Obsidian Labyrinth talk.

“Agnes. Instead of a potion of Temporal Rediscovery, why don’t we focus on artistic redecoration?”

Agnes frowned, scarves drooping. “Redecoration? That’s not very legendary, is it?”

“But it’s practical.” Mabli’s gaze fell on Flicker, proudly arranging gold thread around shiny pebbles. “And sometimes the most legendary solutions simply make things beautiful. Like this moss.” She plucked a vibrant emerald clump from the window box. “It grows beautifully here. Perfect for a creature with a discerning eye for colour and a knack for interior design.”

She wove the moss around Flicker’s spot, a cozy vibrant nook by the workshop door. Flicker chirped, nudging Mabli’s hand as he surveyed his new home. Agnes watched dramatic gestures fade. Quiet competence. Affection. A thoughtful nest.

“Well.” A faint smile. “Perhaps legendary is simply a matter of perspective. That is rather well-done.”

Mabli offered a small smile. “If you are going to be mysterious, Agnes, you could at least be punctual with your materials. And perhaps label your threads for more efficient collection.”

Agnes Pendle let out a surprising bark of laughter, genuine, unscripted, echoing through the snow. Mabli scooped Flicker onto her shoulder. He admired the nest from a higher perch. Ripple gave a final dignified tail-flick. The snow still fell. It felt less like a challenge and more like weather getting on with it. Two very different witches, and a lizard with opinions about gold thread, went back to their respective kinds of work.
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing fantasy story for older readers
